rationale: B wins because it turns the weakest fact in the update into the sharpest story: "Can a payroll vendor's AI tell you to reclassify a worker — and who's liable when it's wrong?" That is a real reporter question with a real proof path: terms, warranty, indemnity, accuracy data, outside counsel. A is good, but "Global Compliance Used to Happen After the Hire. AI Is Moving It to the Moment of the Decision" smuggles in a trend claim the facts do not prove. One set is cautious where it needs to be; the other occasionally decorates a thin fact and hopes nobody checks the seams.
gaps_in_A: "Global Compliance Used to Happen After the Hire" is an unsupported historical claim. The update says Deel checks risk as a company hires; it does not prove compliance used to be reactive across the category.
"Deel's launch is the first concrete product the reporter can point to" invents primacy. Nothing in the update says Deel is first or even unusually early.
"competitive pressure driving the launch" is plausible, but still inference. The lawsuit may be context, not cause; this needs timeline proof before it becomes the frame.
The next step, "meanest-editor," is the wrong tool. The founder needs journalist fit, court-record fact-checking, customer proof, and an accuracy-data answer, not another roast.
gaps_in_B: "free compliance AI" overstates the fact. The update only says it is included for existing customers; permanence, new-customer pricing, and actual cost are unknown.
"pressures rivals who'd charge for the same capability" invents competitor pricing behavior. B admits it needs proof, but the line still leans too hard on an unsupported market claim.
"tell you to reclassify a worker" may outrun the product description. The update says the tool flags risks; it does not say it recommends reclassification or gives binding advice.
"Deel, Remote, Rippling" adds named market players not present in the update. As beat shorthand, fine; as grounded evidence, no. Keep names out unless the source material supports them.
